articles.title: Current-Driven Molecular Machine with Rotation-Enhanced Conductance
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 22 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11312-xCurrent-Driven Molecular Machine with Rotation-Enhanced Conductance
articles.content: For more than two millennia, Archimedean screws have been used for water pumping and, more recently, as turbines in hydroelectric power stations[1]. Their helical-blade structure, essential to their function, is also found in chiral molecules and nanostructures, where injected electric current has been proposed to generate torque-mediated rotation[2,3]. Here, we present a torque-driven molecular machine with a rotor actuated by electric current and conductance enhanced by its rotation. Suspending a helicene molecule between two electrode tips, we show that an applied voltage induces cyclic molecular motion with 100% directional preference that can be inverted by the voltage’s polarity. Above a voltage threshold, the current through the rotating molecule is significantly enhanced, and the enhancement onset is tuned by stretching or compressing the helical molecule. Such effects were absent in previous helical molecular junctions, likely due to structural and operational differences[4–6]. Calculations show that molecular rotation by current-induced forces explains both the observed cyclic motion and current enhancement. This mechanism predicts a transition from stepwise to continuous rotation at a threshold voltage, yielding a current increase as rotation allows adopting highly conducting configurations not accessible at rest. Our work introduces a prototype for a new class of torque-driven molecular machines with perfect rotor unidirectionality and significant current modulation.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant breakthrough in molecular machines, demonstrating a current-driven molecular rotor with enhanced conductance and controlled directional rotation. This innovation represents a meaningful advancement in nanotechnology with potential broad applications in electronics and molecular machinery, impacting technology development at a fundamental level.
articles.personality_title: Scientists create tiny molecular machine that spins and boosts electricity flow
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For thousands of years, Archimedean screws have moved water using a spiral shape. Similar spiral shapes, called helices, also appear in very small molecules. Scientists thought electric current might make these tiny spiral molecules spin, but it was not proven.

**What happened** – Researchers built a tiny machine using a spiral-shaped molecule called helicene, placed between two tiny metal points. When they applied an electric voltage, the molecule started spinning in one direction. Changing the voltage direction made it spin the other way. When the spinning started, the electric current flowing through the molecule increased a lot. Stretching or squeezing the molecule changed the voltage needed to start the spin.

**Impact** – This is the first time scientists have made a molecular machine that spins perfectly in one direction powered by electricity and also improves how well electricity flows. This discovery helps us understand how to make very small machines that can be controlled by electric signals. It could lead to better electronic devices or tiny machines working inside materials.

**What's next step** – Scientists will explore how to use these spinning molecules in real devices. They want to see if they can combine many molecular machines to do useful tasks, or improve how electronics work at the smallest scales.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new molecular machine spins in one direction powered by electricity and boosts current flow, opening doors for future tiny devices controlled by electric signals.

articles.title: Can maths survive AI? Fields medallist Terence Tao calls for a ‘Maths 2.0’ world
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 22 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03389-1As machines race ahead in solving problems, mathematicians must establish a new era that prizes human understanding over simply publishing more solutions.
articles.content:
Advanced artificial-intelligence models are transforming mathematics at an astonishing speed. In the past few months, AI-aided proofs — logical arguments that demonstrate why a mathematical result is correct — have been released for hundreds of long-standing maths problems.

Mathematicians might need several months to fully understand the underlying arguments and implications of these automatically derived solutions. As a mathematician who uses AI tools for my own research, I can see that the field has fundamentally transformed. We now urgently need to establish a ‘Maths 2.0’ era, in which ‘proof scarcity’ is no longer a defining feature of the field.

How AI is reshaping discovery in maths and physics

The challenges associated with this new way of doing maths are already evident. Many AI-generated results are not described clearly enough to meet quality standards for publication. Some researchers using AI tools simply move on to the next problem once they have a minimally presentable proof, leaving results that can be difficult for other mathematicians to assess. And it still remains unclear how extensively AI models are drawing on the previous work of mathematicians without providing proper attribution.

The centuries-old practice of openly sharing maths problems is under serious threat because mathematicians are increasingly fearful that disclosing their research directions will lead to their work being ‘scooped’ by a rival who is equipped with a frontier AI model. Graduate students and junior mathematicians used to develop their skills and gain early recognition from their peers by solving such problems. On 6 October, technology firm OpenAI dumped hundreds of solutions to such problems online in one go. It disrupted countless research programmes overnight.

Perhaps the most counter-intuitive consequence is that human understanding of mathematics is falling behind, because AI systems generate results faster than mathematicians can digest and absorb them. Confined to pure mathematics, this ‘proof indigestion’ might be a minor concern. But AI-generated mathematical models deployed in the real world without a matching understanding of their mechanisms could have serious consequences. For example, complex AI-generated models are already used to some extent to determine who qualifies for a bank loan and to measure financial risk in markets. If the complexity of these models outpaces the capacity for humans to understand when they might malfunction, the risks of unforeseen mistakes will grow, affecting the general public.

‘It is incredible’: How AI is transforming mathematics

These negative impacts are not inevitable. Used creatively, and with the right incentives, AI tools could enhance human understanding. It is still possible to change course, through a radical reassessment of the conventional incentive structure of mathematics and by introducing more-responsible practices around AI use.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a transformative breakthrough in mathematics driven by AI, emphasizing the potential for AI to accelerate problem-solving and reshape the field significantly. It addresses broad implications for society, including risks and opportunities, and calls for responsible adaptation to harness AI's benefits while preserving human understanding. This represents a meaningful, large-scale impact on science and technology with societal relevance.

articles.title: Scientists turned art detectives date van Gogh's 'Starry Night' to actual night sky in 1889
articles.summary: A team of South Korean researchers has put forward a new date for the night sky depicted in Dutch painter Vincent van Gogh's famed masterpiece "The Starry Night". Art historians have long assumed the stars were a product of the artist's fantasy or dated the scene to June 1889 based on the artist's known location and other factors, but astronomical details like the sliver crescent moon didn't line up.
articles.content:
Scientists doubling as art detectives have traced Vincent van Gogh’s painting “The Starry Night” to a celestial scene that suggests a new date for one of the world’s most famous paintings.

Their findings indicate that rather than being a product of van Gogh’s imagination, “The Starry Night” may have been inspired by what he saw as he gazed heavenward from his French asylum 137 years ago.

A South Korean team reported Thursday that after years of forensic astronomy and research into the Dutch artist, they have matched his masterpiece to a predawn sky over France’s Saint-Remy de Provence right around July 22, 1889.

That’s a month later than the long-accepted time frame for the postimpressionist painting depicting a crescent moon and Venus surrounded by a sky of swirling stars with a village nestled below and cypress trees looming on one side.

Read moreClimate activists target art: Van Gogh’s masterpiece 'Sunflowers' defaced

Art historians have long dated the painting to June 1889, soon after Van Gogh checked into the asylum. He’d cut off his left ear several months earlier during an argument with painter Paul Gauguin.

A team led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, the CEO of a Seoul telescope maker, is now disputing that date in a study appearing in the journal Scientific Reports.

The sky that is most similar to the painting occurred around July 22, 1889, said Kim, who is also a doctoral candidate at Kyung Hee University. He noted that the few days before and after could have inspired van Gogh as well.

“No two skies are the same. Something always changes. I believe Vincent noticed those changes and put them into the painting,” Kim said in an email.

He added: “I am confident that July 22 is the better date. I will bet on this date.”

The latest study addresses “a real puzzle” that in mid-June 1889, the moon was not the thin crescent painted by van Gogh, said Jose Luis Aragon at the National Autonomous University of Mexico. He has studied “The Starry Night” as a physicist, but did not take part in the new research.

“Still, I would see the July date as an intriguing hypothesis rather than a settled answer,” Aragon said in an email.

Long fascinated by van Gogh’s art, Kim traveled to France in 2019, the first time in mid-June and the second around July 22. He found brilliant stars rising in July’s predawn sky, unlike June.

Kim and his team discovered through further celestial sleuthing that around July 22, 1889, the shape of the moon before dawn appeared like the one in the painting, with the Hyades star cluster in the constellation Taurus rising in the east alongside Venus. The sky should have been clear enough for van Gogh to see all this, based on their weather analyses.

Van Gogh is thought to have suffered a seizure around that time in July. But Kim and his team contend that the seizure occurred later in July, based on their analyses of letters between the painter and one of his brothers. Some of those letters refer to cicadas, another clue that points toward the hotter July, according to Kim.

The researchers tested and verified their methods on night skies in other paintings, making for what Aragon considers “a careful and genuinely interdisciplinary study”.

Read morePostcard provides clue to exact spot of Van Gogh’s last painting, says researcher

Since van Gogh painted in a studio at the asylum from sketches and memory, “the sky is likely a composite of many nights as the authors themselves acknowledge", Aragon said.

“What I find most convincing is the broader message: The painting is not pure fantasy. Van Gogh watched the real sky very closely," Aragon said.

Despite all his research, Kim has never seen “The Starry Night” at the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

“Now that the paper is out, I really have to go and see ‘The Starry Night’ in person, don’t I?” he said.

(FRANCE 24 with AP)
articles.source: News and stories on CULTURE, movies, music, literature - France 24

articles.title: The Indian workers filming their work to train AI
articles.summary: Indian workers are being paid to film themselves at work and the footage is used to train AI.
articles.content:
Mohammed Ashim has been cutting hair and trimming beards for four years in Bengaluru.

But recently the 22-year old has been strapping a camera to his head to record his work.

The camera only records his hands and fingers - his client's faces are blurred out.

"The routine is simple, but you have to be disciplined about how you move. The operations team taught me that my hands always have to stay cleanly inside the frame, the lighting has to be sharp, and I can't tilt my head too abruptly while working."

He wears the camera for five or six hours a day.

"It's good money, but honestly, the feeling of doing something this futuristic is what keeps me excited. I never imagined my razor techniques would be useful to a global tech company," says Ashim.

He is one of hundreds of thousands of workers across the world paid to record their activities.

Ashim's footage is collected by a local company, which might have hundreds of people filming their work.

That video is then sold on to technology companies and research organisations who use it to train artificial intelligence - in particular so-called physical AI, a type of artificial intelligence that can control robots in the real world.

Rashdan Technologies collects and processes such human generated data.

"Every robotics company, every frontier AI lab, has a specific kind of data they want: industrial tasks, agriculture, household chores, small business work like pottery, garment-making, embroidery, candle-making. We go wherever the task is," says co-founder and CEO Shahil Baig.

His company pays $5 to $10 (£3.74; £7.47) for eight to 10 hours of recorded work.

"For a lot of these people, that's meaningful," Baig says.

Making sure workers give their consent and are comfortable with the process is important, he says.

"We record hands, not faces, and where multi-camera rigs do capture more of the body or environment, we blur faces out. No names, no contact details, nothing that identifies them personally goes into what we hand off."

But his customers are getting more demanding.

"Now clients are asking for four to six cameras rigged around a person's head to cover the entire scene, not just the hands.

"Getting someone to agree to one small camera is one conversation. Getting them to agree to wearing what's effectively a five-camera headset is a completely different, and harder, one. We pay more for that tier of data collection because of what we're asking of people."

And the industry is becoming more crowded, Agarwal expects dozens more competitors to emerge in India this year.

articles.personality_title_es: Trabajadores indios graban sus habilidades para entrenar robots
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En Bengaluru, India, trabajadores como Mohammed Ashim, un barbero, están grabando videos de sus manos mientras trabajan. Estos videos se usan para enseñar a sistemas de inteligencia artificial (IA) a realizar tareas físicas.

**Qué pasó** – Mohammed, de 22 años, lleva una pequeña cámara en la cabeza que solo graba sus manos mientras corta cabello y recorta barbas. Lo hace durante cinco a seis horas al día, siguiendo reglas estrictas para mantener sus manos visibles y desenfocar los rostros para proteger la privacidad. Sus videos son recogidos por una empresa local, Rashdan Technologies, que paga entre 5 y 10 dólares por 8 a 10 horas de grabación. Luego venden estos videos a empresas de IA y robótica en todo el mundo.

**Impacto** – Este trabajo ayuda a entrenar un tipo especial de IA llamada IA física, que permite a los robots realizar tareas del mundo real como trabajos industriales, agricultura o artesanías. Al usar videos de personas reales, la IA aprende con más precisión. Los trabajadores ganan un ingreso significativo y su privacidad se protege desenfocando los rostros y sin compartir datos personales.

**Próximo paso** – Las empresas quieren videos más detallados, a veces usando varias cámaras para capturar toda la escena. Esto significa que los trabajadores podrían usar equipos de cámaras más complejos en el futuro, por lo que recibirán un pago mayor. La industria está creciendo rápido en India, con muchas nuevas empresas que comenzarán proyectos similares.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Trabajadores indios ayudan a enseñar nuevas habilidades a robots grabando sus manos en el trabajo, ganando dinero y apoyando avances en tecnología de IA.
